hypothesis: The per-option calculations are independent, so a static OpenMP partition should improve throughput for large n when the caller allows multiple threads. Keeping the existing serial routine for a one-thread budget avoids team-creation overhead there; clamping the requested team size to n avoids creating workers with no outputs. No candidate measurement is available, so any speedup and whether this variant should be kept remain for controller evaluation.

The Black–Scholes iterations are independent, so an OpenMP SIMD-only loop may expose their arithmetic and CND sign selection to compiler vectorization without adding scheduling. Reusing sqrt(T) within an iteration also avoids repeating it in d1 and d2. Scalar libm calls remain legal fallbacks when vector transcendental support is unavailable, so a speedup is uncertain. The baseline is correct at the supplied cases with mean 0.0025316 s; the available baseline record does not separate timing by size or budget.

Horner evaluation of the existing CND polynomial should reduce its multiply/add work, and caching sqrt(T) and v*sqrt(T) should remove a repeated square root per option. These are algebraically equivalent transformations, but changed floating-point rounding may affect tolerance; speed and correctness remain to be measured.

With the selected parent’s sqrtT and vSqrtT sharing held fixed, replacing the Horner recurrence with explicit k²…k⁵ terms tests whether Horner’s dependency chain contributes to the measured slowdown. The explicit terms may expose more independent scalar work, but may also cost more operations. Expect a repeatable latency reduction over the parent if that chain matters, particularly at n=262144; test correctness and time at n=32768 and 262144 with thread budgets 1 and 4. Reject on any fixed-tolerance failure; stop pursuing this form if it has no repeatable large-size improvement.

With the baseline’s explicit CND polynomial and all other calculations held fixed, computing sqrt(T) and v*sqrt(T) once per option and reusing them tests whether explicit common-subexpression sharing helps beyond what the compiler already does. If the compiler does not already eliminate the repeated work, expect a repeatable time reduction, most visibly at n=32768 and n=262144; otherwise time may be unchanged or regress. Check fixed-tolerance correctness and timings at both sizes with thread budgets 1 and 4. Reject on any correctness failure and stop pursuing this sharing if it has no repeatable large-size benefit.

This parity-split, Estrin-like CND polynomial is a materially different scalar mechanism from the recent full-Horner and explicit-power variants. Sharing k² between odd and even coefficient groups may reduce arithmetic and expose independent work; the changed floating-point evaluation order may affect tolerance, and compiler optimization may eliminate any speed benefit. The falsifiable test is fixed-tolerance correctness and wall-time comparison at n=32768 and n=262144 with thread budgets 1 and 4; reject it if incorrect or if the large-case timings show no repeatable benefit.

The prior valid candidate's OpenMP static worksharing loop was faster than baseline at four threads on the supplied larger cases, while its one-thread cases were slightly slower (ca5ac26dfa9f4c7a; baseline-e1). This candidate tests a contrasting mechanism: one OpenMP team with explicit contiguous ranges derived from each worker's actual team size, rather than a worksharing loop, while retaining the direct serial path for threads <= 1 and capping the requested team at min(threads,n). I expect identical outputs and possibly lower multi-thread scheduling overhead; reject it if correctness or output coverage fails, if the thread budget is exceeded, or if its end-to-end timings do not improve reproducibly over the measured static-loop candidate.

The earlier SIMD-directive-only candidate was valid but slower in aggregate than the baseline (0.002704 s versus 0.002532 s), while still relying on scalar libm calls. This contrasting candidate explicitly packs four lanes for Black–Scholes arithmetic and the CND polynomial, but deliberately evaluates logf, sqrtf, and expf lane by lane. It may reduce scalar arithmetic overhead at larger sizes; the added packing and scalar transcendental work may instead erase any gain. Reject it if correctness or tail/alignment checks fail, or if repeated timings show no improvement over the scalar baseline at the larger supplied size.

Change only the CND polynomial from an explicit power sum to Horner form, retaining the repeated sqrtf expressions and all other calculations. This isolates the polynomial change from the recent Horner-plus-sqrt-sharing variant. The reassociation may reduce arithmetic, but compiler optimization or floating-point rounding may erase a benefit or affect tolerance. Compare correctness and repeated wall time against the base and e037 at n=32768 and n=262144 with thread budgets 1 and 4. Reject on any fixed-tolerance failure; stop pursuing this form if it does not show a repeatable improvement over e037 in both large-size configurations.

Pre-scale the CND polynomial coefficients by the constant normalization factor so it can be folded at compile time, leaving only the exponential multiplication per CND call. This tests a distinct scalar mechanism from the recent Horner, parity-split, and sqrt-sharing attempts; it may save one runtime multiply per CND, but coefficient rounding or compiler optimization may erase the benefit or affect tolerance. Compare fixed-tolerance correctness and repeated wall time at n=32768 and n=262144 with thread budgets 1 and 4. Stop if correctness fails or there is no repeatable improvement in both large-size configurations.

Factor the existing CND polynomial into two short groups, k*(c1+c2*k) + k^3*(c3+k*(c4+c5*k)), reusing k^2 and k^3 and avoiding explicit k^4/k^5. It may reduce multiplications, but changed float association could affect tolerance and compiler optimization may remove any benefit. Request fixed-tolerance correctness checks and repeated timing at n=32768 and n=262144 with both thread budgets; do not assume a speedup or exhaustive correctness from a finite suite.

Adding a general serial cutoff at n <= 128 tests whether avoiding OpenMP team startup improves small-call latency, a mechanism not tested by the prior candidates' n <= 1 cutoff. Falsifiable test: check correctness, full output coverage, and budget behavior at n=2, 17, 128 and non-divisible larger sizes, with budgets 1, 2, 4, 8 and threads > n; compare timings at both supplied sizes and budgets. Reject this variant if correctness or budget checks fail, or if the measured end-to-end result does not improve against relevant measured alternatives.

Test a distinct combination of two previously measured scalar CND ideas: put the existing degree-five polynomial in Horner form and pre-scale each coefficient by the normalizing constant, leaving only the exponential multiplication after the polynomial. This may reduce runtime arithmetic, but changed float association and coefficient rounding may affect tolerance, and compiler folding may erase any benefit. Prior Horner and coefficient-scaled variants passed the finite correctness suite, while their aggregate timings were close; their results do not establish the behavior of this combination. Reject on any fixed-tolerance failure or absent repeatable improvement, comparing repeated wall times at both supplied sizes and thread budgets.

The valid manual contiguous partition (e730c0133bd74895) and default static worksharing loop (ca5ac26dfa9f4c7a) had similar measured means, so this tests a distinct partition granularity: static cyclic chunks sized for about four chunks per requested worker. If per-element math-library costs vary enough to leave workers unevenly loaded, this may reduce large-loop imbalance while retaining contiguous work within each chunk. Test correctness, full output coverage and budget behavior at budgets 1, 2, 4 and 8, including n=3 with threads=8 and n=17 with threads=4, and compare repeated end-to-end timings at n=32768 and 262144. Keep it only if it is correct and improves reproducibly over the best measured alternative; otherwise stop without claiming a gain.

Retain the selected parent’s parity-split CND polynomial and explicitly compute sqrt(T) and v*sqrt(T) once per option for reuse in d1 and d2. Retain the selected parent’s Horner CND polynomial and change only its multiply-add stages to scalar fmaf calls. The two distinct valid T2 candidates measured so far provide a useful contrast: the SIMD directive-only version was slower in aggregate than baseline, while the explicit four-lane version was faster in aggregate, though the scoped comparison reports a small-size regression at one-thread budget. This experiment uses the same lane-wise scalar logf/sqrtf/expf fallback and vector CND polynomial/arithmetic mechanism, but widens the explicit block from four to eight lanes. It tests whether wider source vectors help the large supplied size or instead incur extra packing/lowering cost; it is rejected if correctness fails or repeated large-size timings show no gain beyond dispersion without acceptable results on the other size/budget configurations.

The selected parent is the explicit eight-lane kernel (valid, correct, aggregate mean 0.0016225 s). Its expensive logf, sqrtf, and expf calls still occur in two scalar lane loops. Add OpenMP SIMD to only those loops to test whether the compiler can lower lane-wise transcendental calls more efficiently while retaining the parent's vector arithmetic, lane width, and scalar tail. A compiler without suitable vector math may show no change or a regression; this is not a presumed speedup. Reject on any correctness/guard failure, or if repeated per-size/per-budget measurements show no gain beyond dispersion on a large case without acceptable results on the other configurations.

The measured four- and eight-lane vector-extension candidates retained scalar sqrtf calls, while the eight-lane candidate had the best aggregate mean (dbc123f349d04f1f: 0.0016225 s) and adding SIMD directives to scalar lane math did not improve that result (93bbe29b49d94541: 0.0016357 s). Unlike prior explicit packed-vector kernels and generic SIMD-loop trials, this candidate asks the compiler to create a SIMD clone of CND and applies SIMD to the scalar Black–Scholes loop. Test correctness and repeated wall times at both supplied sizes and thread budgets; reject on any correctness failure or if the timing benefit is absent or inconsistent.

The selected parent relies on compiler SIMD around expressions that still call scalar libm, while prior packed arithmetic left both CND exponentials lane-wise. Retaining the selected eight-lane parent, this experiment targets its remaining CND cost: both Gaussian exponentials are still scalar expf calls inside lane loops. Replace only the two CND Gaussian expf calls with an inlined range-reduced degree-nine Taylor evaluation and power-of-two scaling, keeping an exact expf fallback for exponents below -80. The expected observation is lower large-case time if the compiler vectorizes the common arithmetic path, with outputs inside tolerance; unchanged or slower timings, or any correctness failure, falsify the candidate. Test correctness and repeated timings at both supplied sizes and thread budgets, including arbitrary tails and output alignments; stop at the first correctness issue or if no repeatable benefit survives dispersion without unacceptable regressions.

On the assigned scalar base, a guarded four-lane SSE2 block can vectorize the Black–Scholes arithmetic and CND rational polynomial/sign selection while leaving logf and every expf exact and scalar per lane. The selected b08 kernel still evaluates each CND Gaussian with scalar expf calls. Replace only that step with explicit SSE2 base-2 range reduction, packed degree-eight exp evaluation on the reduced interval, and exponent-bit reconstruction; retain exact expf for out-of-range lanes, plus the existing scalar non-SSE and tail paths. Correctness failure, or no repeatable improvement over the selected parent across supplied sizes and thread budgets, falsifies the benefit hypothesis.
